planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to partial shade once soil has warmed after frost; keep dry once the leaf yellows in fall.

directions: Remusatia vivipara is a summer-growing Himalayan and Australian aroid best known for an unusual self-propagating trick: after its single arrow-shaped leaf dies back in fall, the dormant tuber sends up odd upright stolons studded with sticky little tubercles that hitch a ride on passing animals or gardeners' clothing to start new colonies elsewhere, giving rise to the common name hitchhiker elephant ear. In late spring, before the foliage emerges, mature tubers push up a small bright-yellow aroid flower directly from the bare ground. Plant tubers in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to partial shade after the soil has warmed, and keep the planting on the dry side once the leaf yellows in autumn, since wet soil during winter dormancy is the most common cause of rot. Where winters run colder than the warmer half of zone 7, lift and store the tuber dry like a caladium.

planting.note: Divide slow-spreading rhizomes in early spring or fall and replant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained woodland soil in part to full shade.

directions: Coiling leaf Solomon's seal is an uncommon Himalayan and West Chinese relative of the familiar garden Solomon's seals, distinguished by narrow leaves held in whorls of three to six around an upright to gently arching stem, each leaf tip curling into a small tendril-like coil. Small axillary flowers dangling in pink-to-cream clusters appear in late spring, followed by blue-black berries that often hide beneath the foliage into fall. Grow it in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained woodland soil in part to full shade, dividing the rhizomes in early spring or fall; in cultivation it typically stays a well-behaved 2-4 feet tall even though wild populations can reach much taller. Protect young growth from slugs and give it a sheltered spot out of drying wind, as with other woodland Polygonatum species.

planting.note: Set divisions near a shrub or modest trellis after frost danger passes, in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in light to partial shade; mulch the crown over winter at the colder end of its range.

directions: Streptolirion volubile, sometimes called climbing spiderwort for its kinship with Tradescantia, is an herbaceous twining vine from the moist forests of East Asia that scrambles up shrubs and tree trunks rather than forming a typical groundcover clump. Slender, twisting stems carry heart-shaped leaves and produce loose clusters of small lavender-and-white, three-petaled flowers over a long season from late spring into fall. It performs best scrambling through an open shrub or up a modest trellis in light to partial shade with reliably moist, humus-rich soil, and benefits from winter mulch at the colder end of its range. Site it where its relatively tender, non-woody stems are protected from hard freezes, since it dies back in anything beyond a light frost and is reliably perennial only in the mildest zones.

planting.note: Divide clumps of tuberous roots in spring and plant in light, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled to partial shade.

directions: Chinese asparagus is an East Asian relative of garden asparagus grown as a shade-tolerant, tuberous-rooted scrambling herb rather than for edible spears; its wiry, climbing stems carry fine, needle-like cladodes, small greenish-white bell flowers, and red berries, giving it an airy, fern-like texture useful for softening shaded trellises or woodland edges. The fleshy, clustered tuberous roots are the part traditionally harvested and dried for use in East Asian herbal preparations, typically after the plant has grown undisturbed for two or more seasons. Grow it in light, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled to partial shade, dividing clumps of tuberous roots in spring; established plants tolerate some drought once rooted in but perform best with regular moisture during active growth. Top growth dies back in hard freezes but resprouts reliably from the tuberous root system where winter lows stay above roughly 5°F.
